procedural_history.originating_court: Special Judge (PC Act), CBI-08, New Delhi (Special Court)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 03.12.2022 passed by the Special Court granting default bail to respondent nos. 1 and 2 under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The CBI, aggrieved by the Special Court's order, filed Crl.M.C. No. 6544 of 2022 before the High Court of Delhi under Section 482 r/w Section 439(2) of Cr.P.C. The High Court, vide order dated 30.05.2023, dismissed the CBI's petition and upheld the Special Court's order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The CBI, as the appellant, approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order dated 30.05.2023 in CRL. M.C. No. 6544 of 2022, which had upheld the Special Court's decision to grant default bail. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The respondents-accused shall be taken into custody in this case, if released on default bail pursuant to the impugned orders.
it is clarified that observations made in this judgment shall not influence the Special Court or High Court while deciding the other proceedings, if any pending before them, on merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether an accused is entitled to statutory default bail under Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, on the ground that the investigation is pending against other accused, even when a chargesheet has been filed against the applicant accused within the prescribed time limit and cognizance has been taken by the court?

facts: A chargesheet was filed against the respondent-accused and 74 others within the prescribed time limit of 90 days.
The chargesheet mentioned that further investigation against some other accused was still pending.
Based on this chargesheet, the Special Court took cognizance of the offences allegedly committed by the respondents.
After cognizance was taken, the respondents applied for statutory default bail under Section 167(2) of the Cr.P.C.
The respondents argued that the chargesheet was 'incomplete' or 'piecemeal' because the investigation against other accused was not finished.
The Special Court and the High Court granted default bail, agreeing with the respondents' argument.
law: Under the proviso to Section 167(2) of the Cr.P.C., an accused acquires an indefeasible right to be released on 'default bail' if the investigating agency fails to file a chargesheet within the stipulated period (60 or 90 days).
This right to default bail ceases to exist once a chargesheet is filed within the prescribed time limit.

The pendency of a 'further investigation' under Section 173(8) Cr.P.C. against other accused or for the collection of additional evidence does not invalidate a chargesheet that has already been filed.

A chargesheet is not considered 'incomplete' merely because investigation against other accused is ongoing. If the chargesheet contains sufficient material for the court to take cognizance of the offence against the accused in question, it is a valid report under Section 173(2).

The court takes cognizance of the offence, not the offender. Once the court is satisfied from the material in the chargesheet that an offence has been committed by the accused, it is immaterial whether further investigation is pending.
application: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the right to default bail is extinguished the moment a chargesheet is filed within the statutory period.
In this case, the chargesheet against the respondents was filed within the 90-day limit, and the Special Court found sufficient material in it to take cognizance of the offences.

The Court reasoned that the ongoing investigation against other accused was merely a 'further investigation' under Section 173(8) and did not make the chargesheet filed against the respondents incomplete or defective.
Therefore, the respondents could not claim a right to default bail on the ground that the investigation, as a whole, was not fully complete for all potential accused.

The Court held that the Special Court and the High Court committed a serious error of law by granting bail, as the necessary conditions for default bail (i.e., non-filing of a chargesheet) were not met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that an accused is not entitled to statutory default bail under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C. on the ground that investigation is pending against other accused, as long as a chargesheet has been filed against the applicant-accused within the prescribed time limit and the court has taken cognizance. The Court, therefore, set aside the orders of the High Court and the Special Court that had granted the bail.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an accused is entitled to statutory default bail under Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, on the ground that the investigation is pending against other accused, even when a chargesheet has been filed against the applicant accused within the prescribed time limit and cognizance has been taken by the court?
appellant_arguments: The filing of a chargesheet against the respondents within the prescribed time limit, upon which the court has taken cognizance, extinguishes the right to default bail under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C.

A chargesheet is not invalidated or vitiated simply because some documents are not filed along with it, especially when those documents were not in the possession of the investigating agency at the time.
The pendency of further investigation against other accused does not render the chargesheet filed against the current accused incomplete for the purpose of Section 167(2) Cr.P.C.
respondent_arguments: The filing of the chargesheet was a subterfuge or ruse specifically to defeat the indefeasible right to default bail conferred under Section 167(2) Cr.P.C.
The chargesheet should be considered incomplete because the investigation was still pending against other accused, and therefore, it does not prevent the right to default bail from accruing.

cases.case_name: Sanjay Dutt v. State through CBI, Bombay (II)
cases.principle: The right of default bail is an indefeasible right that flows from Article 21, but it is enforceable only prior to the filing of the challan or chargesheet and does not survive or remain enforceable once the challan has been filed.

cases.case_name: K. Veeraswami v. Union of India and Others
cases.principle: To explain the scope of Section 173(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

A statute must be read in its entirety to give effect to all its provisions. So long as a charge-sheet under Section 173(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not filed, the investigation remains pending, but the filing of a police report does not preclude an officer from carrying on further investigation under Section 173(8).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An accused cannot claim the statutory right to default bail under Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure on the ground that investigation is pending against other co-accused, if a chargesheet has been filed against the applicant accused within the prescribed time limit and cognizance has been taken.
obiter: The indefeasible right to default bail is enforceable only prior to the filing of the chargesheet and does not survive or remain enforceable once the chargesheet has been filed.
A court takes cognizance of an offence, not the offender.
An investigating officer is not precluded from carrying on further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure after a police report has been filed.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The statutory right to default bail under Section 167(2) of the Cr.P.C. ceases to exist once a chargesheet is filed against an accused within the prescribed time limit and the court takes cognizance of the alleged offences. The pendency of further investigation under Section 173(8) against other accused, or for the production of documents not yet available, is immaterial to this right. Such pending investigation neither vitiates the chargesheet filed against the applicant accused nor renders it 'incomplete' for the purposes of Section 167(2), and therefore cannot be a ground to claim default bail.
legal_tests_applied: The primary test is whether the indefeasible right to default bail was enforced by the accused prior to the filing of the chargesheet (challan). The right does not survive or remain enforceable once the chargesheet has been filed, if not already availed.

Once a chargesheet is filed, the question is whether it is sufficient for the court to be satisfied about the commission of an offence and to take cognizance. If cognizance is taken, the condition for extinguishing the right to default bail is met, irrespective of whether further investigation against other individuals is pending.
policy_considerations: The court adheres to the procedural principle that what cannot be done directly should not be permitted to be done indirectly. Granting default bail after a court has already taken cognizance of the offence based on a chargesheet would be an indirect method of recalling the order of cognizance, an action a magistrate ordinarily cannot take.
